claims.claim: The Romantic period in Western art music is often placed roughly from the early nineteenth century to about 1900, with overlapping boundaries and continuing Romantic-style influence afterward.

Romanticism in nineteenth-century arts is commonly associated with imagination, intense emotion, individuality, freedom, nature, and connections among music, literature, and visual art; no single trait defines every work.

Romantic composers continued inherited genres such as symphony, concerto, sonata, and opera while developing or enlarging repertoires including art song, piano miniatures, and instrumental program music.

A common listening profile includes lyrical melodies, expanded chromatic and dissonant harmony, wider dynamic and timbral contrast, flexible tempo, and either short intimate or large-scale forms; these are tendencies rather than universal rules.
Nineteenth-century orchestral forces expanded in size and instrumental color, and virtuoso performers became prominent in public musical life.

Program music uses instrumental sound to evoke or represent a nonmusical subject such as a story, scene, poem, painting, or event; an interpretation still needs evidence from the work and its context.

positions: Some OER surveys use a broad nineteenth-century frame or approximately 1820–1900.
Some composers and works are described as late Classical, early Romantic, post-Romantic, or early Modern.
